Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to seek the permission of the House to move a motion on a matter of pressing and urgent necessity.
In view of the clear statement by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) last Thursday as reported on pages 3965 and 3969 of Hansard that the Special Joint Committee on the constitution could make its own decision on televising its own proceedings, and in view of the fact that on August 22, 1978, the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) ruled, when chairman of the Special Joint Committee on the Constitution of Canada, that committees did not have the power to authorize the televising of their own proceedings, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker):
That the Prime Minister direct his House leader to bring a motion before the House authorizing the televising of the proceedings of the proposed Special Joint Committee on the proposed constitutional resolution.

subsubtopic: DORCHESTER, N.B.-CALL FOR PUBLIC JUDICIAL INQUIRY-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43 in connection with certain recent events at Dorchester Penitentiary in New Brunswick.
In view of the allegation of the shooting of hundreds of prisoners in a crowded gym by a number of prison guards in June of this year, in view of the escapes of four convicted murderers, in view of the tragic death of a prison guard at Dorchester Penitentiary and the suicide of a prisoner, and finally, in view of allegations of beatings and gassings of prisoners both before and after the tragic hostage-taking incident, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong):
That this House call upon the Solicitor General to commission an independent, public, judicial inquiry into all the recent serious and tragic events at Dorchester Penitentiary in recent months.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Right Hon. Prime Minister. I should like to ask the right hon. gentleman a question, a little sadly but seriously. In 1964 on the university stage as a professor, one Pierre Trudeau wrote:
-federalism is ... a pact or quasi-treaty in the sense that the terms of that compromise cannot be changed unilaterally.
Earlier this month, on television, the right hon. gentleman said:
Every member of Parliament from every corner of this land is asked to participate in this historic act.
Oral Questions
He was referring to the debate. On the political stage, however, the Prime Minister has acted unilaterally and has choked off debate. Could the right hon. gentleman please tell this House what role he intends to play when he goes west tomorrow? I am glad that he is going west and I hope he travels around other parts of the country. However, could the Prime Minister tell the House what role he intends to play and give us one good reason why we should believe anything he says, either in the west or in the east?

INQUIRY WHETHER DISCUSSIONS HELD BETWEEN PRIME MINISTER AND LIBERAL LEADER IN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to put a question to the Right Hon. Prime Minister. Might I point out to him that the proposal he made last week at least allowed the constitution to be amended here in Canada, by Canadians, instead of through the intermediary of the British government.
As the Prime Minister is aware of the result of the referendum and is now committed to the promise he made at that time; as Mr. Claude Ryan said, in light of the proposal of the Prime Minister of Canada on the way to patriate the constitution, that if he had been told all he had to do was to listen to what the federal government is now saying, in a letter to the editor of the newspaper Le Devoir which the Prime Minister must surely have read, that he would never have been chairman of the No committee; and as last Sunday, the leader of the opposition in Quebec, Mr. Ryan felt obliged to ask the British parliamentarians to reject the request of Ottawa, I therefore conclude that there has been very little communication with the Prime Minister; and as the Prime Minister repeated yesterday, to a question put to him, that he did not know whether Mr. Ryan would change his mind, that he had no way of knowing; under the circumstances it seems that communications are totally lacking between the Prime Minister of Canada and his Liberal colleague in Quebec, and chairman of the No committee-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER DISCUSSIONS HELD BETWEEN PRIME MINISTER AND LIBERAL LEADER IN QUEBEC
speechtext: Order. Is that the question of the hon. member, that is, that communications-would the hon. member put his question?

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER DISCUSSIONS HELD BETWEEN PRIME MINISTER AND LIBERAL LEADER IN QUEBEC
speechtext: Right away, Madam Speaker. Can the Prime Minister tell the House whether, after the federal-provincial conference, he had the decency to discuss with his Liberal colleague who chaired the No committee, in view of some of the proposals contained in the Beige Paper, his decision to act unilaterally, a decision which had already been contested by his Liberal colleague in Quebec?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER DISCUSSIONS HELD BETWEEN PRIME MINISTER AND LIBERAL LEADER IN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, since the preamble to the hon. member's question was fairly lengthy, I will reply to it in the terms I have just used to answer his colleague from the maritimes.
The hon. member is blaming us for disagreeing with Mr. Ryan because we are proceeding unilaterally. 1 think those are the words used by the hon. member for Joliette. I remind him that last May or June the House unanimously passed a motion introduced by one of his colleagues, the hon. member for Edmonton West I believe, which indeed suggested that Parlia-
Oral Questions
ment move to patriate the constitution. That resolution said nothing about provincial agreement. I indeed suggested that they should at least be consulted, which was done, of course, throughout the summer. But the motion introduced by the hon. member for Joliette and his colleagues asked for patria-tion by way of a resolution of this House and not by way of a resolution passed by the ten provinces. That is the first point.
The second point is, as I have already mentioned, that last week the hon. member himself voted for a resolution put by his leader asking that this House patriate the constitution, with an amending formula of course, but without the consensus of the provinces. So what is he complaining about? Of a unilateral patriation which he himself and his party have already endorsed?

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER DISCUSSIONS HELD BETWEEN PRIME MINISTER AND LIBERAL LEADER IN QUEBEC
speechtext: Madam Speaker, if I may-and this is very important-1 shall remind the right hon. Prime Minister that our proposal required that amendments be made here in Canada, by Canadians and for Canadians. The Prime Minister stopped short of saying so and he has not answered my question either. Considering the present situation in Quebec, the embarrassment the proposal is causing their Liberal colleagues in Quebec and the respect we have for Mr. Ryan's proposals, does the Prime Minister intend to disregard the appeal Mr. Ryan has made for a re-evaluation and reopening of negotiations with the provinces instead of asking the British parliament to rule on fundamental rights for Canadians, which should be done in Canada? I ask the Prime Minister, Madam Speaker, if it is his intention at least to try to get the support of his Liberal colleague in Quebec instead of dividing the forces, as is now the case.

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER DISCUSSIONS HELD BETWEEN PRIME MINISTER AND LIBERAL LEADER IN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 cannot hear without being amused the member who pleads that the Liberals should not tear each other to pieces. Madam Speaker, the member has sat on this side of the House as an independent. If he is so much interested in the union of my forces, he should leave his hypocritical party which suggested a unilateral patriation last week and which this week condemns us when we proceed in such a way. As for our intention to make amendments in Canada, Madam Speaker, this is the purpose of our resolution since from 1953 we have been unable to patriate our constitution, so that all major amendments made since then, whether they deal with unemployment insurance, the admission of Newfoundland in confederation, etc., have been legislation passed in England and not in Canada. Now, the procedure which we are following is not new, it has been in effect since 1867. All the amendments voted by the House must be ratified in Great Britain. This is exactly what is being proposed today, that it be considered and put to a vote in the House and then voted on in Great Britain, as has been the case for 113 years.

subsubtopic: PROTECTION OF WORKERS UNDER FEDERAL JURISDICTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Labour. As a result of a one-week tour by the NDP caucus committee on occupational health and safety to the maritimes, we were shocked to learn of the state of anarchy in the field of health and safety caused by the fact that jurisdiction over health and safety is spread over 13 government departments and agencies, resulting in neglect of workers' safety and their lives.
I would like to ask the minister what specific measures he plans to correct this jurisdictional problem and to bring federal legislation up to provincial standards so that the one million workers under federal jurisdiction can receive the same level of protection as their provincial counterparts.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for the question, but I think he will have to be more specific as to his area of concern. It is quite true that the ten provinces under our constitution have substantial responsibilities in areas of safety and health in the workplace because of the limitation of federal jurisdiction in labour. I certainly do not agree with the premise in his question that federal laws provide any less of a level of safeguard to the safety and health of workers than do the provincial jurisdictions' acts. There is a great variety-

subsubtopic: PROTECTION OF WORKERS UNDER FEDERAL JURISDICTION
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: PROTECTION OF WORKERS UNDER FEDERAL JURISDICTION
speechtext: If hon. members opposite would just settle down a bit, they might be able to deal with this matter better. There is a great variety of provisions in the various provinces on the subject, but the hon. member will be aware of the fact that in mining, for instance, as a federal government we are responsible only in the case of the uranium mines in Ontario and Saskatchewan and in the case of coal mining through our ownership of Devco in Nova Scotia. October 28, 1980

room for negotiation, that the federal government had locked up the budget and that the Prime Minister implied that it would be very inconvenient to alter it, why did the Prime Minister refuse any further discussions with Premier Lough-eed because they would inconvenience his timetable? I thereupon considered whether I would meet Premier Lougheed or not, and I repeat that I invited him to come down to meet me yesterday on this subject. The point is that I did not want him to come under the illusion that there would be major changes in the budget made at that point. I think even hon. members opposite will realize that the budget, which was going to be brought down eight days after I received the letter, was pretty far advanced in its preparation. So in fairness I told Premier Lougheed that I would be happy to see him, but if he had really wanted to suggest major changes I imagine he would have written me sooner than eight days before the budget was to be brought down.
There were discussions earlier in the month of October between ministers when the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources-I believe on October 2 or 3 or thereabouts-went west and made a whole new series of proposals which were turned down. They were still open until, I would say, about the 1 5th of the month. But the hon. member and the House should realize that by October 20, since the budget was being brought in on the twenty-eighth, we were pretty close to a final package. I had to be quite frank with the premier on that, but I assured him that the budget would contain many pleasant surprises and that if he wanted to have a preview of them, he would be welcome, although it is probably contrary to the principle of budget secrecy. Since our provisions do impact in a very particular way on Alberta, I would have been prepared to give him a preview of the budget yesterday, which is well in advance of the usual timetable.

We have succeeded in implementing broadcasting in the House of Commons, and in my view this decision still holds. Consequently, I am of the opinion that the joint committee which will be established will have the power to determine whether or not it wishes its deliberations or proceedings to be broadcast. THE LATE HON. JUDY V. LaMARSH

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the passing of the Hon. Judy LaMarsh, the Parliament of Canada and the people of Canada lost a friend, one who served her country well in war and peace.
Judy LaMarsh-or Judy as she was known far and wide- loved this House, loved the cut and thrust of debate, loved the challenges she had to grapple with on behalf of the people of Niagara Falls but, more than that, on behalf of all the people of Canada.
Carrying out her legislative responsibilities, many of them controversial in nature, certainly was not easy for her. She had to battle a tough opposition here in this chamber, and not always across the aisle-sometimes within the ranks of her own party. She had to do battle with the provinces on a number of occasions. She had to do combat with the media. But she was never one to back away from a fight, as anyone
October 28, 1980

who knew her can attest. She approached such challenges with relish. And this, of course, was characteristic of her approach to everything. Grab hold of life was her belief; pour all you can into it, get all you can out of it in the way of real satisfaction.
What made thousands of Canadians Judy LaMarsh fans was her great zest for living, her great humanity, her willingness to pour her heart out for a friend-indeed loyalty to friends was a great part of her credo-but, above all, her gusty, no holds barred performance in the arena of public life.
I said she loved this chamber. She knew how to work with it. Eler friendships cut across party lines often, but she was a faithful partisan in the best sense of the word.
As a minister, she had a record of legislative achievement that few others could match. She helped set the social and cultural structures that remain her monument to this day: the Canada Pension Plan, the Canada Assistance Plan, medicare, the Broadcasting Act, Status of Women in Canada, and the Centennial year celebrations. All of these attest to her ability, her enthusiasm, her concern for people and, above all, her vision of Canada.
It was not always easy for her, but at a time when few women were active political figures she dominated the political scene in Canada. She was an inspiration to many others, and will remain so.
Courageous, controversial, warm-hearted, determined; she was all of these, and more. She always knew she had a job to do and she did not pussy-foot around it. She got on with it. And when things did not always go her way, she came to terms with that and got on with something else.
I saw her several months ago in hospital when she knew that her remaining time was limited. She had come to terms with that also. "After all," she said, "1 never wanted to be old and alone and a woman". Judy LaMarsh never will be old and alone. She will be remembered by thousands of Canadians as someone who contributed greatly to the betterment of our society; she will be remembered by members of this Parliament as a loyal friend, a tough opponent, a courageous parliamentarian, a dedicated Canadian. Madam Speaker, she will be sorely missed.
All hon. Members: Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, on behalf of my colleagues in the New Democratic Party, I should like to join in the words you uttered yesterday and with the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) in the tribute she paid just now to the memory of Judy LaMarsh. Seldom have I heard words of tribute so well expressed as those just spoken by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands. We all join in the sentiments she expressed.
I had the honour of meeting Judy LaMarsh for the first time on the day she took her seat in this House of Commons following a byelection 20 years ago this month. During the time she and I were both members of this House, I had a great deal to do with her because of our interest in social and other
Tribute to Former Privy Councillor
legislation. She made a mark on the history of this country that will be remembered for a long time.
As only the second woman to be a member of the federal cabinet, she pioneered in that area and millions of Canadians, for generations to come, will be grateful for the benefits of the Canada Pension Plan which was put through this House because Judy LaMarsh stuck with it in spite of a considerable amount of opposition of which some of us were aware.
We got to know her as a warm and friendly person. It hit us hard to learn that she had to end her days with so much suffering from such a serious illness and to die at such an early age. But life is measured not by its length but by its quality and its contribution. In those terms the name of Judy LaMarsh stands high in Canadian history, and we pay our tribute to her memory today.
Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, on behalf of the government and members on this side of the House, I am very honoured to have the opportunity of offering a few words of respect for the Hon. Judy LaMarsh.
I did not have the pleasure of sharing moments in the House of Commons with Judy because she left Parliament shortly before I arrived in this place. I have known Judy LaMarsh for more than two decades, however. I believe that 1 would not be in this House today, Madam Speaker, were it not for my activities in my own party at the University of Toronto in 1960, when I had occasion to meet Judy LaMarsh at a meeting in my home town of Kitchener. It was the spirit, the independence and the drive of Judy LaMarsh that led me to believe that if a member of Parliament could have all those traits, have so much fun in her system, be so full of goodness and be so principled, then to follow an interest in politics and perhaps a political career in the future would be a desirable thing.
Judy LaMarsh was a distinguished minister in this party. She was the first woman to serve in a Liberal cabinet. She served in two senior portfolios, as minister of national health and welfare and also as secretary of state, distinguished herself in both, and is particularly remembered for her role in the introduction and passage of the Canada Pension Plan, as other members have mentioned. Perhaps 1967 was the year of the first real awakening among Canadians from coast to coast that they could be proud and could respect our character, culture and diversity. Indeed all the things we seemed to discover about ourselves in centennial year were in the spirit of Judy LaMarsh, the minister who made that such a success.
When I met Judy LaMarsh she was not discouraged by the plight of our political party at that time. She was never discouraged in her fight that women should have a more just position in political life in Canada. In the last year or two she faced a terrible trial. Again, Judy's wonderful courage and

October 28, 1980
Privilege-Mr. Shields
ambition to succeed in the things that she believed in, life, health, and caring for others, once more carried her through.
If I may, I would just like to add the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) issued yesterday when we all received the sad news. This statement is dated October 27, 1980, and reads as follows:
I was deeply saddened to learn today that the Honourable Judy LaMarsh had finally lost her courageous struggle with cancer.
We are left, however, with many vivid memories of Judy-as a cabinet minister who developed Canadian social security into a program which is now the envy of the world-as the master impresario of Canada's great centennial celebration-as a successful and respected lawyer-as a committed champion of womens' rights-as a best selling author and, of course, as a deeply involved Liberal partisan.
No tribute from me would be complete without reference to Judy's characterization of me at the 1968 leadership convention. Even when it was at my expense,
I could not help admiring her colourful and frank style, which was always accompanied by an ongoing sense of dignity and a large measure of good humour.
Judy LaMarsh lived her life as a Canadian in full measure, and for this we can all be grateful.
Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, on behalf of the people of Niagara Falls riding 1 wish to thank this House for its condolences on the untimely death of the Hon. Judy LaMarsh. Her passing is a time of great sorrow for Canadians everywhere. She served her country with distinction both in war and in peace. Hon. members will understand when I say that in Niagara Falls her loss is very great indeed among her people. Our feeling of sadness is very personal, and will be with us for a long time.
We appreciate your kind words of sympathy, Madam Speaker, and the tributes expressed to the voice of Niagara, which is now silent.
Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, I spoke during debate on this bill last Friday, and I would like to conclude my remarks now.
This legislation contains many of the measures that our party, through my colleague from Brandon-Souris, has advocated for a number of years. As 1 pointed out on Friday, the best intent of my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser), seems also to be reflected in the bill. 1 repeat that I support this bill and look forward to its passage.
As I said last Friday, I oppose closing rural post offices on Saturdays. They are very important to the people of my riding, and I am sure they are equally important to rural Canadians across Canada. Because of the distances that many rural people must drive to get to post offices, the time constraints of farm life, and often stormy weather of Canadian winters, days of opening of rural post offices should not be curtailed. Rural Canadians depend on their post offices six days a week and 1 know they will not welcome Saturday closings.
Those members in this House who represent large rural ridings like mine, will know that in many of the towns and villages that dot their constituencies, the local post office is the only visible symbol of the federal government. The red and white sign outside the building names the postal station, and the Canadian flag flies proudly above. To close rural post offices on Saturday would not only cut off access to the mail, it would also serve to drive a wedge between rural Canadians and the only visible symbol of the federal government in their community.
I hope the new corporation will take a look at the condition of some of the rural post offices in Canada. In my riding the Denbigh post office is in a private home. Although 1 have made representations to post office officials to have a new station built, I believe the new corporation should look closely at this situation and adopt a policy of building post offices to replace postal facilities located in private homes, where the volume warrants.
It is my sincere hope that this bill will address the many serious problems that currently plague the Post Office. The matter of labour-management disputes has to be considered the most important of these problems. Other important issues
October 28, 1980

include electronic funds transmission, as my colleague, the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale), referred to in his remarks on Friday. Should this new technology become a widely accepted practice, as many people believe it will, the result will be devastating for the Post Office. It will mean a very significant decrease in the volume of first class mail handled by the Post Office. This will result in a great loss of revenue and, perhaps, more important, will mean a loss of many jobs for postal employees.
The tension between labour and management over this issue will become more serious. As management responds to this decrease in the use of the Post Office, they will certainly have to cut jobs that have become obsolete. Job security has always been a thorny issue for labour-management negotiations, and we can expect that situation to continue if the electronic transmission of funds becomes a reality.
If further instability results in the Post Office, it will inevitably mean more lost revenue, pushing the Post Office debt up even higher than its current debt of $485 million. Every time there is a disruption in postal service, the private courier services pick up more customers. Many of these customers are not temporary, they are permanent. This results in even less use of the Post Office, meaning even more lost revenue, less need for postal employees, and more opportunity for labour-management strife. The result is a vicious circle.
I mention this because it is a real problem that the new corporation has to deal with. I might add that I do not envy the responsibilities of the members of the board of the new corporation. They are inheriting a mess. The government has learned the fine art of incompetence over the past decade in its management of the Post Office. It has perfected this art during the debate on the constitutional resolution. It is this legacy which the new corporation will have to address, and 1 wish them the very best of luck in putting the Post Office back on track.
Before I conclude, I would like to mention that I deeply regretted the day that the government dropped the name of "The Royal Mail" for the Post Office. In the minds of many people this may not be a matter of much significance, but to me, Mr. Speaker, it is a reflection of an attitude which has invaded many quarters of the government that has resulted in the loss of many references to the tradition of the monarchy in Canada.

When it comes to plant maintenance and so on, we switch over to Public Works. These bureaucratic complications have certainly caused problems in labour-management relations. The Clark government was in the process of preparing legislation to create a Crown corporation when the election was called last December. There have been numerous studies since 1962 which recommended converting the Post Office into a Crown corporation. As I have already mentioned, Bill C-27 was introduced to convert the Post Office into a Crown corporation. It did not receive second reading. The Progressive Conservative Party objected to the bill because it proposed a two-tier system of management. We felt that such a system would aggravate labour-management relations.
The problem facing the Post Office and some of the reasons for conversion were as follows. First, there was a decline in the reliability and efficiency of the Post Office over the past ten years. Approximately two or three years ago the hon. member for Brandon-Souris and I visited post offices in Europe, principally the post office in Great Britain. automatic equipment, but besides making employees as mad as the dickens, it also did not speed things up, as we are all aware.

The first and most important concern is with respect to clause 5(2) of this legislation. As the minister pointed out in his opening remarks on Friday, this is far and away the most important provision in the bill. This clause guarantees that Canadians will continue to enjoy basic customary postal service. Naturally we agree with that sentiment, but we are not sure what is meant by basic customary postal services. Does the government mean that all Canadians living in residential communities over a certain size will continue to receive daily home delivery of mail, or does it mean that all letters will be sent to some large green box in the middle of the neighbourhood and that Canadians will have to trudge through the ice and snow to pick up their mail? I ask this question in all seriousness because in a large number of large Canadian cities, especially in western Canada, that is what basic customary postal service has come to mean.
Does this phrase mean that rural post offices will continue to stay open six days a week, or does it mean that the new corporation will follow through on this government's promise to reduce service by at least one day a week? Does this phrase mean that some rural towns on the Canadian prairies will be able to keep their post offices and, through that, their only link with the federal government, or does it mean that these small post offices will be closed?
This phrase will be considered very carefully by judges in the not too distant future when they will try to determine whether or not the new corporation is adequately fulfilling its mandate. Quite frankly, we are concerned that a judge might not interpret this wording in quite such a wide manner as the minister did on Friday when he introduced the bill. For that reason, Mr. Speaker, we will be proposing amendments to this clause in committee which would clearly spell out what is meant by customary postal service. I am sure that if the
minister is as concerned with this issue as he was on Friday, he will have no problem in supporting our amendments in committee.
Our second major concern with this legislation is in clause 22(2). This clause is very short and, on the surface, does not appear very serious. All it says is that the new corporation will be able to enter into any contracts it likes. The problem with this clause, quite frankly, is that it gives the corporation the power to dismantle the Post Office altogether. Let us say, for example, that the corporation's board decided that it did not like its letter carriers' union. Under this clause it could simply tender a contract with some firm, pay the firm a set amount of money, and let them worry about finding letter carriers and paying them a fair salary. This is not a wild idea since it is already occurring in several communities across the country. We are finding that Canada Post is going into the contract business with unscrupulous businessmen who are hiring cheap labour to deliver the mail at the minimum wage. The government is able to stop worrying about labour relations, the contractors are making money hand over fist, and the workers are being shafted. For there to be any kind of labour co-ordination in the postal service once Canada Post becomes a Crown corporation, it is very important that we look into these problems.
Under this provision in the legislation the corporation will be able to contract out virtually every function with which it is being charged. This is not a reasonable situation and must be corrected before the bill is out of committee. We will be proposing an amendment to the effect that the corporation will not be able to contract out any work which, by its very nature, is an essential part of the postal service.
Our third major concern focuses on clauses 14 and 15 which deal with the exclusive privileges of the corporation. Naturally we agree with the government that the Post Office must have a monopoly over the delivery of letters, but we cannot understand why they have decided to allow the continued use of private parcel post delivery systems. Our argument is very simple and we hope that the government will pay heed to it.
Everyone knows that parcel delivery is the most profitable area of postal service. It is in this field that the Post Office makes up for its losses in the delivery of letters. Clearly, it is more profitable to deliver a parcel across town than it is to deliver a letter to Old Crow in the Yukon. By letting private couriers compete with the Post Office in parcel delivery, we are letting them skim the market. We do not let the railways skim the market, nor do we let the airlines skim the market, so why on earth should we let United Parcel Service and Purola-tors Courier Service skim profits from the Post Office? All this will mean is that letter rates will go sky high, especially since the government has announced its intention to make the new corporation self-sufficient.
United Parcel Service has decimated the postal system in the United States. I beg the government not to do the same thing here in Canada. I hope that hon. members opposite will support my proposal to amend clause 14 to ensure that parcel post delivery remains the exclusive privilege of Canada Post.

I have looked in vain for a definition of that phrase and I do not know whether it means the elimination of the basic service we have today, and whether or not it will put an extra burden on our rural people and on many of our urban people to whom mail is delivered customarily. It is difficult enough now at times without making it any more difficult, and 1 hope the minister, when he closes the debate on this bill, or in committee, will give us a definition of "maintaining basic customary postal service."
1 wonder if the practice that has been followed for many, many years in the Post Office of keeping a post office open when other businesses are open will be included under the definition of basic customary postal service. Today there is a move on foot to close the rural post offices in our towns and villages on Saturdays. These days Saturday is not the business day it once was in many parts of this country. But Saturday is still a very important day and many rural people go to town on Saturday to do their shopping, and expect to get their mail. 1 strongly urge when this thing is being considered that we don't simply say we are going automatically, and in a blanket way, to close all post offices on Saturdays. Many people work long hours, from the early morning until late at night, to make a livelihood for themselves and their families. I have some correspondence to indicate that the only time a person has to go to the post office and do his postal business is on a Saturday.

Another point in connection with basic service which bothers me is the hours of work. Today, for instance, in our Calgary post office, it operates from 7 a.m. to 5.15 p.m. Out in Airdrie, just a few miles away, the Post Office does not open until 8.45 a.m. So that means workers cannot get there and do their postal work before they go to work, and it is closed by the time they finish their work day.
I would like to suggest that the major aim of the Post Office should be to serve the people of this country, to get them their mail and give them service of which they can be proud. Several years ago there was no difficulty in the Post Office. You mailed a letter with the utmost confidence that it would reach the person to whom you addressed it within a very short period of time. Now we have no such assurance at all; it may get there in three days or it may take 17 days. This is not good enough, and if that is going to be the basic postal service which we have today then we are not going to satisfy anybody by simply calling it a Crown corporation. 1 think it is very important to realize that changing the name and changing some of the set-up may not have the desired effect. That in itself is not going to give us good postal service. There must be some very basic changes made in the present set-up.
One of the things about this bill which worries me a great deal is the constancy with which I see the words "appointed by the minister", or, "with the approval of the minister", or, "shall be appointed by the governor in council". The president, chairman and directors are all appointed by the governor in council to hold office during pleasure. Are these people going to be responsible to the cabinet or responsible to the people of this country?
We already have a situation where the minister is responsible to the people through this House, and I am wondering if this is going to put them beyond the reach of this House. Will we be able to consider the difficulties which may arise with regard to post office services? Will we be able to represent the people who send us here by having someone to whom to direct our questions? At the present time we may ask the minister, and the minister endeavours to answer our questions. If there is something wrong he can take steps to have it corrected. Are we putting the Post Office beyond the reach of the people, through their elected representatives? If so I am not going to like it at all.
We must have definite assurances that we will be able to make representations, that those representations will be heard, and that those who are appointed as chairman, president and directors are to be responsible to the people by reporting to the members of the House of Commons. I think that is a very basic and important item.
Another point of concern to me is that of the chain of command. If this bill is not going to alter the chain of command I do not think we will see any improvement in our postal service. In my view that is one of the basic things wrong with the present postal service.

A regional post office takes a great deal of blame, such as the Calgary regional post office, and in my cases properly so. The mail from Edmonton is delayed in Calgary for sometimes as long as seven days-I am told-before it gets through Calgary, which is where the bottleneck takes place. But you cannot put the whole blame on the regional post office in Calgary because the director there has no authority. If he has a poor employee who is not doing his job he must write to Ottawa. I was informed, on good authority, that it is sometimes three months before a reply is received from Ottawa. By that time eveyone has forgotten what the incident was about and why the man should have been discharged on the spot.
Unless your employees are responsible right down the chain of command you will not get good service. Whether it is a business or whether it is a government department, there must be a chain of command. The head of that, the president or chairman of the board, should be able to put his finger on the person who is causing the hold-up. Sometimes it is the management at fault, not the workers at all.
I was amazed when I was informed that during the last public service strike the managers of one of the regional post offices in Toronto were all going to work even though there was no mail being delivered. The security was all there even though there was no mail to protect and no employees present to do the work. The upper echelon went each day and played cards, and got paid by the taxpayers. 1 do not think that is responsible at all. Surely the taxpayers should not be ripped off in that way. If the workers are not in, then we should not be paying the managers to be there. That is one of the difficulties today; there is no chain of command in our Post Office. Almost everything has to be directed to the top in Ottawa. The simplest things have to be done that way, and this costs a lot of money and causes a lot of concern.
No wonder workers get frustrated when they see somebody slacking on the job while they are working full time doing their utmost to earn their pay, while beside them the person sloughing off is getting the same pay. And nothing is done about it because no one is responsible. They must write to Ottawa and say "Mike is not doing his job, may I fire him, please?" Or "May I slap him on the wrist?" Or "May I discipline him?" Surely if we are going to have a Crown corporation we should look to private enterprise as an example. Private enterprise would not put up with that. They would not stay in business if they did. And whether it is a Crown corporation or a government department, we should not put up with it either.
The chain of command is something which I will be watching very carefully as the legislation comes into operation. 1 hope that the chairman, president, and the board of directors will give that matter a great deal of attention because this is one of the things which today is causing chaos in our post office system.
We invested thousands of dollars to get automation in our Post Office. I am told that there is equipment which has been purchased, costing several thousands of dollars, and it has never been used. It has never been used and it is still silting there. Again, that tells me there is no chain of command.
Nobody is taking the responsibility, and that should not happen. This instance can be supported time and again across this country. 1 raised the matter in the Standing Committee on Public Accounts two years ago. I was amazed at the representatives of the Post Office who seemed to think that everything was okay.
These occurrences also happen in Toronto. There was an incident there where a little screw caused the shutdown of an automatic machine. The operator went out and bought a screw for 15 cents and installed it in the machine. The machine was fixed and it started to work again. This man was reported to management because it was felt that he had done something terrible.
He was called before management because they wanted to know why he had taken this action. Management told him that the next time he would be discharged if he did such a terrible thing. This individual should have followed procedure, written out a requisition for the screw and taken it to the office. It would probably have been sent to Ottawa, then things would really have been screwed up and the machine would have been out of work for three weeks. When we hear about incidents like this, it is no wonder that we are not getting our mail. A chain of command must be established. If people such as this workman wish to do something well, then let us congratulate and commend them, not tell them they will get fired the next time they go out and buy a 15 cent screw.
Another thing which bothers me about the post office is that there seems to be no vision toward the future. Somebody said the other day that where there is no vision the people perish. I can take hon. members to post offices across this country which were built just two years ago, three years ago and five years ago, and which today are unable to cope with the amount of business. I realize that in some places there is reason for this inability to cope.

There is also the fact that they must travel the distance to the post office. There is an underpass for the people on the east side of the highway, but they still must go the distance to the post office. The underpass is there as a result of the efforts of the Alberta government, not of the federal government. In any event, they are not getting their mail, so they are unhappy and there is discontent.
Again, if there is a chain of command, surely there can be the vision that when a town begins to grow the post office should immediately increase its service, the same as private enterprise would do in such a situation. If a private entrepreneur were operating a store and saw that he could not handle his customers, he would expand and build another store, and another, to serve his customers. That is what the post office should do, serve the people.
Another example is the town of Okotoks. There the post office is in a Crown-owned building, but there are not enough boxes. Again, the town has grown and grown, and there are subdivisions. When subdivisions become evident around a town, why are steps not taken to provide boxes for those subdivisions? There are no boxes, and the people of that town stand in line for general delivery. Yet the Post Office says to people, "You cannot expect to get your mail unless you have a box", and these people cannot buy a box for love nor money. The town of Strathmore is another case. I have pointed out three very definite cases where the evidence was there but nothing was done.
1 do not blame those who ten years ago did not foresee this eventuality, but I certainly blame those who did not foresee the occurrence of such a situation in the last two years, three years or four years, when the situation became more evident all the time. Now we have the situation, for example, in the town of Airdrie where 10,000 people are trying to obtain their mail from a little post office. There are no boxes, and these people must stand in line for 45 minutes.
How would the hon. members of this House like to stand in line every day for 45 minutes? Let us bring it down to our own case and see how we would like it. These people have things to do. They are earning a living for their families.
I am also bothered by some of the ridiculous regulations which are introduced, not to give better service to the people, but to give them poorer service. There are post offices which follow the directive from somewhere in Ottawa that if a box number is not on a letter it must be returned. Thank goodness there are also some postmasters who have enough common, ordinary horse sense that when they receive a letter for John Jones without a box number, they say, "Well, I know John Jones because he has lived here for 25 years. I will put it in his box".
There is a postmaster in my own riding who returns the mail because there is no box number. How in the world can Mary Jane living in Toronto know the box number of Harry Jones in Airdrie if it is the first time she has written to him? These
Canada Post Corporation Act
postmasters should use a little, ordinary, common horse sense.
It would solve an awful lot of problems.
I am also bothered a great deal by the fact that the Post Office chisels on its smaller post offices. The postal workers in these places are not paid the same rate as people in the larger centres, yet they have more responsibility. For instance, there is a post office in my riding of Bow River which has been provided by the postmistress who has pulled in a trailer. This trailer is now costing her a great deal to operate. If the Post Office officials did not want to provide a building and accepted her offer to provide a building, why were the terms of rental not worked out before she pulled the trailer in and had it converted? Rather, the Post Office has told her that they will not even pay her enough to meet the monthly payments on the trailer. There is also the wages of this postmistress who is paid at the rate of $2.50 per hour. In larger centres the employees receive $7.50 per hour.
Larger centres have supervisors and people to audit and check the books. In small post offices the whole thing is done by the postmaster. And because they are a small post office, we chisel on them so that they can hardly make a living. Some businesses depend on how much mail they receive. The mail takes so long to get through the regional post office that those who can afford to pay and who should be doing their business at the post office cannot afford the loss of time, so they rely on private couriers. This has taken a tremendous amount of revenue away from the Post Office.
Each hon. member should look at the matter from the perspective of his own riding. In many small towns in the southern part of my riding some businesses have lost more than half of their business because the mail takes too long to arrive. Businesses such as grain elevators and insurance companies cannot afford to pay the price of couriers. An agent in Turner Valley told me that the Post Office was ruining her business. She said that she could not expect her clients to wait for the assurance that their house, car, or whatever it is they are insuring, is covered. They may wait as long as seven days before the mail arrives, when one could walk the distance in less than a day.
These are the types of things that we have to consider-and we must always consider people. Let us not say that the smaller post offices are hurting the system; in fact, we are hurting them. They provide an excellent service and we need them, and we need to have them open on Saturday as well, Mr. Speaker.
When it comes to the use of automatic equipment, Mr. Speaker, I think we must realize that there will always be parcels that are not properly wrapped. The problem is, however, that even those that are well wrapped take a severe beating as they travel down the delivery trays and bounce along the conveyor belts.
I have here a letter from a friend and constituent, an excellent school teacher, who spent some time in Hawaii. On his return he wrote to me about his problems with the Post

October 28, 1980
Canada Post Corporation Act
Office and I forwarded the letter to the Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet). Among other things, he wrote as follows:
1 solicit your aid in seeing that the correct personnel are made aware of the utter disgust I feel toward the Canadian postal system. Not only is it an inept, bungling department of national disgrace, but a large number of its personnel have no ability to work with the public.
He went on to say:
We shipped five parcels and all five arrived damaged, some of them utterly destroyed.
Surely we can expect better than that from our postal service, Mr. Speaker.
The letter continues:
For example, we packed a dried crab shell in feathers in a box 10 times its size. The box was wrapped in brown paper and butcher twine yet the shell arrived in 33 pieces. When I complained, I was told to take my complaints to the U.S. post office. I shipped a box of books on July 25th, totalling 18 books and magazines. The parcel arrived on September 10th, totally demolished and numbering 9 books.
Half the books had disappeared, Mr. Speaker. It is no wonder the Canadian public is disgruntled in the face of such service.
The letter goes on:
How long is this national disaster going to be allowed to waste tax dollars and destroy property?
In turn, I asked the Postmaster General-how long?
Later in his letter he refers to an occasion when he was expecting a letter which took from August 20 to September 10 to reach him in Strathmore from Humboldt. Yet it only takes eight hours to drive to Humboldt, Mr. Speaker. He goes on to say, "I have just about decided to throw in the towel." That is because he thinks no one cares.
Surely the government should sit up and take notice when hard working people who contribute to the good of this country come to the conclusion that no one in the government cares.
At the present time it takes from nine to 17 days for a letter to travel from Edmonton to Strathmore.

Thank you for your ruling, Mr. Speaker. 1 appreciate it. I chose that method of introduction because it speaks to the sense of wonderment in me as to whether what I have to say about the Post Office bill might be listened to by hon. members opposite. I have watched the debate proceed, and on relatively few occasions have there been more than ten members present. If we on this side of the House are to fulfil our role as the official opposition, I think it is important that we be able to speak on those parts of a bill that we agree with and also on those parts with which we disagree. I also think there should be enough people in the House who have influence in the government caucus, to listen and pay attention.
We are at second reading stage of this bill-the debate in principle-on the desire of the Government of Canada to change the operation of the Post Office and to create a Crown corporation that will manage and hopefully straighten out the postal service in Canada.
I think it is interesting to note that a version of this bill first appeared in the House of Commons in October, 1978. Now, almost two years later, we are still at the first stage of debate. One of the privileges that we have as members of this House is that of making amendments at this stage. The normal process to be followed with bills is that when we complete debate in principle, the bill then goes to committee where we can speak to it as often as we want. There is no time limit at committee stage and amendments can be accepted. The bill then returns to the House for third reading with full and complete debate and, possibly, some amendments, and there is an opportunity to speak on those amendments. This is the process that has

October 28, 1980

been followed for some four years with the Bank Act and, as you know, Mr. Speaker, that is not yet concluded.
We follow this procedure with government legislation because this House, representing the people of Canada, has a responsibility and a right to examine the legislation for its strength and its weaknesses, so that the laws which govern the people of Canada will have desirable rather than undesirable consequences.
It is interesting to contrast the foregoing with the nine weeks from the time the new constitution first saw the light of day to the use of the Post Office to send a resolution off to England. The most fundamental law in this country was debated for 24 hours in this House of Commons without any guarantee of further debate. That is quite a contrast when dealing with fundamental law versus the care and attention that should rightfully be given to this bill regarding the Post Office.
I appreciate what the Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet) said when he opened debate a few days ago. With remarkable candor he told the House that ten years ago-and I am almost repeating his words verbatim-the government moved too quickly to institute a modernization program. The consequence of the quickness of that move is plain to everybody in 1980. Are Canadians happy with their postal service? The answer is no. Are Canadian workers who work in the Canadian postal service happy? The answer is no. Is the management of the postal service happy? The answer is no. The present Postmaster General identified for us the irregular, spotty service, which many members could address. Certainly new members of Parliament get many letters on the inadequacy of the Canadian postal service. Strikes and the staff turnover are the outcome".
The minister told us that employees back in 1970 were not sufficiently informed about the changes coming about. He did not tell us that sufficiency of information might not have been enough, or that the quality might be important. In his introductory remarks the other day he said that a wise postmaster general in 1970 would have and should have had the full co-operation of the postal leaders. He neglected to say, although I think he might concur, that with wisdom modernization should have proceeded, not just with the full co-operation of labour leaders, but with the full co-operation of postal workers.
It is self-evident that the Post Office can only succeed if the people who work within it are willing to commit themselves to it. I suggest that is not unlike a nation, a nation intending to undergo radical change as a consequence of an act taken in secret which is not unlike what happened to the postal service of Canada. This is something which the little people-the ordinary people whom my friend from Bow River mentioned in his speech-might begin to resist and rebel against. I wonder then if that kind of thing happened and as that kind of thing grows whether we have the kind of Canada we had before. Certainly our experience in the Post Office suggests that in
Canada Post Corporation Act
this decade we have not had the kind of postal service that we had before.
The minister has told us the root cause was an inadequate decision taken in haste, without consultation, co-operation and support. Yet that same minister sat here last Thursday evening and helped to cut off the consultation process and freedom of speech in this chamber so that the resolution would proceed without an opportunity for all points of view to be heard. We are dealing with the fundamental law in this nation which will affect the lives of each and every Canadian in frightening unknown ways. If we knew the ways, I would feel more comfortable.
The minister told us in his introductory remarks that that "procedure was very wrong". I ask him, although he is not paying much attention because he is reading a letter, whether he might just reflect on his introductory remarks and their application to something as fundamental and important as the Constitution of Canada.
The minister told us the treatment in 1970 in the Post Office was so quick that "employees felt threatened and pressured". Quick action, lack of consultation, these things can be applied today to Canada. Canadians each day are feeling more threatened and more pressured. Their political leaders are feeling more threatened and more pressured. If the people who worked in the Post Office of Canada ten years ago were asked whether it was their intention to separate from the Post Office or to quit their jobs, had a Gallup poll been taken the answer would have been no. But the Post Office the workers were committed to was pulled out from under them in secret and without consultation. They resisted. The level of service deteriorated, the number of strikes increased, and with it a terrific turnover in staff. The workers did not leave the Post Office, but a decision arrived at in haste took the Post Office out from under them.
I suggest that we are about to engage in a very similar process with the Constitution of Canada. The patriation process and more important, the amendments which are being smuggled through because they are not well understood, are likely to give us the same kind of consequences.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I was encouraged by the Postmaster General's statement that the bill before us today was discussed sentence by sentence and word by word, and all the wording has been well thought out so that there can be no confusion or misinterpretation. He said the bill is not perfect, but it represents the collective efforts of those who will be most affected by it, those who work for and manage the Post Office and who represent the employees through their unions.
It is incumbent upon us to look at Bill C-42 and judge whether the minister's comments about the care and attention of the wording are relevant. We must go one step further and assume, because of our recent history in the House, that the bill before us, as with the constitution act of Canada, will become law. In that light there is a provision which says that that law shall be paramount. Therefore, any other law, including the one before us today to create a Crown corporation, will be subjected to the test of the constitution act, 1980. If the bill we are being asked to consider here today, Bill C-42, to create a Crown corporation for the Post Office, is found to be contradictory to the constitution act of Canada, the bill before us, or relevant portions of it, will be declared to have no force and effect.
If that were to be the final consequence of the passage of this bill, and if it were to have no force and effect, we would
October 28, 1980

have wasted the time of the House. We would then have to reconsider, redraft, and start again. It is in that context that we must begin to wonder whether these carefully crafted and carefully worded sentences really do attend to the will of Canadians as members opposite tell us the constitution act expresses that will.
One of the problems the minister identified is the problem of staff morale. Can we get adequate people, can we keep them, will they be happy and productive? By bringing forward this legislation the minister is telling us that by creating a Crown corporation we will be in a better position to recruit staff, train them, retain them and keep them efficient. However, I have to wonder if these employees will be happy working for a Crown corporation, in effect an extension of the government under the provisions of the constitution act, 1980.
I gave as an example clauses 15(1) and (2), which deal with discrimination rights. I pull one out of that bill. It says we shall not discriminate on the basis of age. Does that have an implication for employees of the Post Office? I do not know, but some people with legal training have told me that they suspect it will.
I raised the issue of whether the only way to deliver money to senior citizens, those who have retired from the Post Office, in the future might be through the application of a means test because all laws in Canada which put age into them will be discriminatory. Our entire life insurance program and our pension plans will be potentially threatened as a result of that one simple provision.
There are other consequences. If postal employees move to a particular community and expect their child to start school at age six and receive a fairly decent education, what if some parents wanting their children to start at age four sued on the basis of this act and the courts ruled that they could not be denied? Say the funds available to a local community to provide schooling have to be provided for four-year-olds as well as five-year-olds, six-year-olds and up. I wonder whether the morale of postal workers would be affected by that kind of provision. I wonder whether the age to drive and the pensionable age would also be affected.
I raise these matters because we do not do this House of Commons or the people of Canada a service unless we examine legislation in the context in which it comes into being and can be enforced. We are examining a postal bill here today with some sense of fear on this side of the House that the social and cultural climate in Canada, the difficulties created by the constitution act, 1980, will reverberate, that this effort and the considerable expense required to change the postal service of Canada into a Crown corporation may in fact be undermined by the simultaneous entry into the Canadian mosaic of a piece of legislation that was not well thought out.
I understand, Mr. Speaker, you are indicating that I have run out of time. I believe I will have the floor to continue the next time the debate comes up.

subtopic: REPRESENTATION AND ELECTORAL DISTRICTS READJUSTMENT ACT (ONTARIO) ELECTORAL REPRESENTATION OF NORTHERN ONTARIO IN HOUSE OF COM MONS
REPRESENTATION AND ELECTORAL DISTRICTS READJUSTMENT ACT (ONTARIO) ELECTORAL REPRESENTATION OF NORTHERN ONTARIO IN HOUSE OF COM MONS
speechtext:
that Bill C-211, to readjust the representation of Ontario in the House of Commons and to readjust the electoral districts in Ontario, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill C-211 before the House this afternoon in private members' hour essentially is designed to ensure that the representation of northern Ontario in this House of Commons would not drop below the 11 seats which now exist from that area of our country. It would set a lower

October 28, 1980
Electoral Representation
limit or a floor under the number of constituencies established in northern Ontario.
The bill is designed especially to counteract the kind of thing which happened in the 1976 redistribution when the number of seats in northern Ontario was reduced from 12 to 11, while at the same time, with the redistribution which took place in the rest of the province, the number of seats was increased from 88 to 95. Of course this bill would not affect the number of seats in any other province. It would only provide a floor of 11 seats as the representation of northern Ontario.
We are concerned with what the Electoral Boundaries Commission, which of course is an independent commission, might do after the 1981 census. Because of the number of seats established after the 1976 redistribution, all but three were in the lower quarter of the population range, that is, the population range in Ontario from 61,000 to 101,000 people. All but three of those constituencies after the 1971 census were in the
60,000	to 70,000 population range.
We are concerned because the population growth between 1971 and 1976 in northern Ontario was .67 of 1 per cent, whereas across the province of Ontario it was 7.2 per cent during the first five years of the decade. Beyond that, the growth trend-of course-would be mainly in the cities, not in the large rural ridings into which most of the constituencies of northern Ontario fall. Even in cities such as Sudbury, which traditionally had a very rapid growth during the early part of the 1970s, in the last couple of years, because of the change in the economics of nickel mining and so on, the population or the number of workers has declined.
Members of the House might ask why we are requesting a floor under the number of seats from northern Ontario. First I point out that northern Ontario is a very distinct geographic area of our country, and certainly of our province. It is important to note that of the geography of the province of Ontario 88.06 per cent of the land mass is located in northern Ontario, and out of the 95 seats for the province only 11 represent that 88.06 per cent of the land mass. It is a big area with 368,800 square miles. For example, the constituency of Kenora-Rainy River, which is the largest in the province, has 148,700 square miles and Algoma, which is the fifth smallest riding in northern Ontario has 13,200 square miles. They are very large constituencies.
It is not only that. For example, the Algoma constituency is about 400 miles long. Literally it is made up of dozens of organized townships, hamlets, villages and Indian Reserves strung out along the Trans-Canada Highway, and various geographic areas like Manitoulin Island which in itself is 100 miles long and 40 miles wide. These small rural hamlets deserve representation and service, but with the population not growing nearly as rapidly as in the rest of the province of Ontario, it makes the boundaries grow larger. Most of these people are far away from government offices, agencies and services. They tend to depend upon their member of Parliament for the many government services which are readily available in city constituencies. Any reduction in the number
of seats would only exacerbate and make the problem that much more difficult.
This bill is supported by all members from northern Ontario, and I believe by all fair-minded people who want to see a reasonable representation from such a large geographical area. Certainly it is supported by the people of northern Ontario who remember what happened in the 1976 redistribution. During the redistribution from 1972 to 1976 there were a number of appeals; there were private members' bills in the House; there were large court battles in which the redistribution was challenged; thousands of dollars were raised in northwestern Ontario especially to challenge the redistribution. I would hope we could do it here in the House of Commons. After all, we are the masters of our own House. We are able to establish a fair and reasonable redistribution arrangement.
I would point out that the Ontario legislature has established or has seen fit to guarantee some 16 seats for northern Ontario in its legislature. I do not see why we cannot do the same thing here and ensure that there is reasonable representation in the House of Commons from this vast geographical area.
I believe this bill will be a fair and reasonable one. I certainly ask all members of the House to support it, so that it can move to committee for further study and discussion.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to add a few comments to my colleague's remarks on Bill C-211. When this matter came before the House a few years ago, I also spoke in support of it. In fact I spoke in support of the suggestion that the 12 seats should remain. Now we are down to 11 seats.
I represent the riding of Parry Sound-Muskoka which, as far as the Ontario government is concerned, is classed as part of northern Ontario. For many years I served on a municipal council. The council would go to Toronto and ask for certain things, and we were told that we were part of northern Ontario. Then when we would go and ask on another basis, we were told that we were part of southern Ontario. I suppose the Parry Sound district is the dividing line between north and south. My colleague will probably get a smile out of this, but I recall at one time saying that we are neither fish nor fowl. I said it seems that the district of Parry Sound is in never-never land.
Northern Ontario is certainly the great bulk of the province, and time and again when I get really annoyed when talking to my southern colleagues, the thing to do is bring out a map of Ontario and point out that little insignificant boot at the south of it which controls the whole thing. I can assure my colleague that 1 certainly support this floor of no less than 11 seats at all times. Again it is the old story of representation by population. That sounds very good in a great many cases, but the geographic angle should also come in. I have also stated time and again that if we went the other way entirely and went on the
October 28, 1980

basis of geography, northern Ontario would be represented as it should be, and our friends in the south would really be crying.
Many times I have spoken to my colleagues who represent that small village of York on Lake Ontario. 1 believe there are 22 members of Parliament from there. Some of the ridings there might be 20 blocks long by ten blocks wide, and some of them not even that. I see my hon. colleague from northwestern Ontario listening with some interest because I know he represents a huge riding. Our urban colleagues from Toronto, Hamilton and, yes, from right here in Ottawa, the capital city, do not know what it means to represent a large area, to try to service it and to try to get around it. That is the reason why I feel that the House of Commons is the place to decide, and the House should say definitely that there should be no less than 11 seats representing northern Ontario. At one time 1 was hoping it would remain at 12.
As 1 came into the chamber from a committee meeting I was talking with one of my colleagues from the New Democratic Party, and he said, "Well, what the hell are you going over there to speak about?" He pointed out that there are 11 seats representing northern Ontario and that the fewer seats there are the better it is for me. In that case we should reduce the representation to just one large seat! I am quite sure that in the years to come the Conservative party will be represented there, but in my view the people of northern Ontario should be represented on a fair basis.
As the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) mentioned, and as 1 believe it to be the case, the minimum is 61,000 up to 101,000. Certainly members of Parliament from those ridings which have 61,000 have a great many miles to travel. The people are greatly in need of the services of members of Parliament and of the various departments. It is not a case of picking up a telephone, like it is in Toronto where there is a regional office or a head office. Therefore it is much more important that northern Ontario be properly represented. 1 see the Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola) nodding in acquiescence. The hon. minister is from Nickel Belt, not Sudbury, and Nickel Belt is a fairly large riding too.
I certainly support this bill. I hope it will be sent to committee and approved so that down the pike-I believe it is in 1981-when there will be another census there will be no way to carve up northern Ontario again, and again take a seat away from it and give it to Hogtown. I like Toronto too, but Toronto has enough seats, and it is very important that the situation be left as it is. If there are to be more seats in the House, a wall can be kicked out, or something. I find no fault with having perhaps a few more seats, but certainly not at the expense of northern Ontario.
When the number of seats was increased from 88 to 95 many of us took a pretty dim view because, instead of southern Ontario getting seven seats, which was the case before, southern Ontario stole one from northern Ontario and now has eight seats. Let us not have that happen again.

Mr. Speaker, in deference to my friend and colleague, the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling), 1 want to remind him that I represent a riding in southwestern Ontario from the centre of which one can drive 17 miles in any direction and be outside the riding. However, I am still standing on my feet this afternoon to defend this bill for my friends in northern Ontario. I want the hon. member who just spoke to realize that not everyone in southern Ontario, the land of milk and honey, forgets about northern Ontario and the problems of that part of Canada.
I should also say at this time that I was born in northern Ontario, so perhaps that is the reason 1 am so sympathetic to this bill.
Before 1 give my reasons for supporting this bill I want to make one or two very important points. We would not have to be worried about northern Ontario and its representation here in the federal House of Commons, we would not have to be worried about the census in 1981 and we would not have to be worried about people leaving northern Ontario, particularly young people, educated people and skilled tradesmen and women, if the federal Liberal governments over the past 20 or 25 years, and the Progressive Conservative governments at Queen's Park, had introduced, established, and implemented industrial strategies for northern Ontario which would have developed that part of central Canada, provided industry, and expanded mining and primary industries using our resources. This would have kept young northerners in northern Ontario.
Instead, due to Liberal neglect federally, and Conservative neglect provincially, certainly many parts of the regions of northern Ontario are slowly dying. All one has to do is go through some of those small and rather pathetic-looking northern Ontario communities, which 20, 30 or 40 years ago were viable economic units, and see them today. As I say, some of them are literally dying, simply because the one company in most of those communities, having finished its mining operations or its logging operations, has picked up and left. The governments either here in Ottawa or at Queen's Park said nothing, and when the one company from one community left, then the young people began to pack it in too.
1 think we should keep those points in mind when we discuss this bill. 1 do not intend to hold it up. I hope it is referred to committee. In fact, I understand that it or its subject matter will be referred to committee. 1 feel that it is virtually impossible or it is becoming almost impossible for members of Parliament to give adequate service to their constituents when the constituencies are so large and disparate and so geographically far-flung. This is what is happening in northern Ontario.
If we reduce the number of ridings, those which are left will become even larger than they are now. 1 hope when the subject matter goes to committee that northern Ontario will be guaranteed the maintenance of at least 11 of the present ridings because if we break up these constituencies or re-draw the boundaries, what will happen is that perhaps one, two or three remote communities which are interlocked socially, ethnically, certainly in a family sense, economically and so forth, will be split off. Heaven knows that today federal members of Parlia-

We have talked about long distance telephone service. We have talked about mail and how slow it is in some of those communities. But I hark back to what I said at the outset. I hope the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), who is on the government side, and other members on the government side will try to press the government, the cabinet, as well as all the backbenchers over there who represent northern Ontario communities, and will make representations at Queen's Park as well, to try to revitalize the economy of northern Ontario so that more people will stay there, not just in Sudbury because of Inco and not just in the Sault because of Algoma Steel, but in all the other communities as well so that they will revitalize and rebuild a once dynamic economy in northern Ontario. We hope people will remain there and that we will not, in ten years time, have to come back and worry about the next census and about more people leaving what is a truly beautiful part of Canada.
As I said, 1 was born in Sault Ste Marie, I lived there for a number of years and I often go back to that part of the country for vacations. 1 have a great deal of respect for northerners, both those in public life and those in private life. I certainly wish northern Ontario well and I hope that the content and intent of this bill will receive the attention it deserves when it goes to committee.
